# Why Ratnasambhava is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *ratnasambhava*. This is the file on how **Ratnasambhava** replaced it.

Ratnasambhava has no biography of battles and loves; as a Dhyānibuddha his 'mythology' is a maṇḍala — a cosmic arrangement in which the south, the color gold, the gesture of giving, and the wisdom of equality converge on a single figure born of the wish-fulfilling jewel.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Ratnasambhava
- **ASCII form:** ratnasambhava
- **Meaning:** "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family"
- **Domain of influence:** Jewel-Born, South
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** रत्नसम्भव
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 414 of 546

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/rɐt.nɐ.sɐm.bʱɐ.ʋɐ/` — 'ruht-nuh-SUHM-bhuh-vuh' — five even syllables, no hard stress; aim the breathy 'bh' in the middle of the word.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Ratnasambhava** lives at [/ratnasambhava/](/ratnasambhava/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/ratnasambhava/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/ratnasambhava/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/ratnasambhava/patterns/).

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

## Where the Name Stood First

The five-Dhyani-Buddha scheme is stamped across medieval Asian sacred geography. At Borobudur in Java (8th–9th century) the galleries distribute the five Buddhas with their characteristic mudrās. In the western Himalaya, the 11th-century temples of Alchi and Tabo preserve five-Buddha wall cycles in which the southern, golden figure displays the gift-bestowing hand. Pala-period (8th–12th century) bronze workshops of the Nālandā region exported small gilt images of the southern Buddha along the monastic routes into Tibet, and Newar craftsmen made the gilt-copper pañca-dhyāni set a fixture of every Kathmandu Valley stūpa — the crowning faces of Swayambhū and Boudhanath still include him. Tang and Japanese maṇḍala paintings preserved at Tō-ji, Shōgo-in, and the repositories of Mount Kōya fix his iconography in silk. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.
